summary: Price County, WI tower with a ladder climb, staffed in 1942 by Leonard Stein and then daughter Betty Stein Murnik; listed as gone, site today undocumented in sources read.

facts.design: Ladder inside the support beams that led straight up, not a staircase
facts.status_note: Listed as gone by the Forest Fire Lookout Association; the Price County Review article names Fifield as the only one of its three towers still standing.

events.note: Leonard Stein ill in fall 1942; daughter Betty (Stein) Murnik took his post at the Elk River tower

evidence.supports: ladder inside the support beams, no staircase at Elk River
evidence.quote: The Fifield and Elk River towers had a ladder inside the support beams of the tower that led straight up.

evidence.supports: Sentinel Point, not Elk River, had the staircase
evidence.quote: At Sentinel Point, there was a staircase.

evidence.supports: Leonard Stein's forestry and lookout service, regular post at Elk River
evidence.quote: Betty's father, Leonard Stein, had worked in forestry and served as a fire lookout for many years, and had a regular post at the Elk River fire tower.
In the fall of 1942, Leonard became ill.

evidence.supports: Betty took her father's place in the tower
evidence.quote: Betty volunteered to take her father's place in the tower

evidence.supports: Betty aged 19 at her first post at Elk River
evidence.quote: Betty (Stein) Murnik was all of 19 years old when she climbed up the ladder into the Elk River fire tower to take her first lookout post.

evidence.supports: phoned the Park Falls office from the cab
evidence.quote: From there, she would phone into the Park Falls office, and settle into her shift of watching for smoke.

evidence.supports: first female lookout in the Forest Service's eastern region
evidence.quote: becoming the first female fire lookout in the Forest Service's eastern region.

evidence.supports: post cut short by returning veterans
evidence.quote: Betty's time serving as a lookout was cut short by the return of veterans from the war.

evidence.supports: Fifield is the only one of the three towers still standing, implying Elk River is gone
evidence.quote: The only one of the towers still standing, the Fifield Tower was built in the late 1920s, and is now on the national register of historic places.

evidence.supports: the article covers three towers (Sentinel Point, Elk River, Fifield)
evidence.quote: who worked in three area fire towers

evidence.supports: veterans' return cut Betty's lookout work short; women's wartime jobs taken back
evidence.quote: Jobs held by women for the duration were taken back and given to the men

evidence.supports: from the cab: the lookout cab that she climbed the ladder to reach
evidence.quote: To access the tiny, seven square foot lookout cab, Betty had to make a long climb up the ladder

corrections.status: applied; facts.agency already reads U.S. Forest Service
corrections.why: The article describes the Elk River lookouts as Forest Service posts; no source read names landmarkhunter as an agency. The name appears only as a bare word on the Forest Lookouts page.

sources.title: Former forest fire lookouts share their memories as fire towers become obsolete

notes_for_editor: One detailed source (the Price County Review article, whose text we read carries no date). No build date, removal date or site condition found, so the story leaves them out. A photo caption spells her name 'Betty Manik'; the body text says Murnik, and the story uses the body spelling. The brief's agency 'landmarkhunter' is corrected to U.S. Forest Service. The brief's 541 m elevation is an OSM ground-elevation tag, not tower height, and is not used. apg-wi.com returned HTTP 429 on a second Price County-area article (Ashland Daily Press, DNR fire towers), so it is unread. Budget note: this tower used three WebSearch calls, one over the cap of two.
